title: Matter and Its Three States
seo_title: Primary 3 Basic Science: Matter and Its Three States Worksheets (NERDC)
standard_code: Primary 3 Basic Science: Living and Non-Living Things
standard_text: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space; it exists as solids, liquids and gases with different properties; matter is made of particles; matter changes state when heated or cooled. (summary of the Basic Science curriculum, Primary 3, theme: Living and Non-Living Things)
meta_desc: Free Primary 3 Basic Science worksheets (NERDC curriculum, theme: Living and Non-Living Things): states of matter, particles in matter, changes of state, properties of materials and matter investigations. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Matter has mass and takes up space.
key_sub: Solids keep their shape, liquids take the shape of their container, and gases fill it.
body_html:
How to think about it

All matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving.

  • Solid: particles packed tightly, fixed shape. Liquid: particles slide past each other. Gas: particles far apart and fast.
  • Heating makes particles move faster: melting, evaporation, sublimation. Cooling: freezing, condensation, deposition.
  • Properties like hardness, flexibility, conductivity and magnetism decide what a material is used for.
Example

Water vapour forms drops on a cold window. What change is this?

gas → liquid

Answer: condensation

Example

When ice melts, does its mass change?

the particles are the same

Answer: no

Common mistakes

  • Thinking air is not matter.
  • Mixing up evaporation and condensation.
  • Thinking mass changes when something melts.

faq.q: What are the three states of matter?
faq.a: Solid, liquid and gas. They differ in how closely packed the particles are and how they move.
A solid turning straight into a gas, like mothballs (naphthalene) slowly getting smaller in a cabinet.
Air has mass and takes up space, so it is matter even though we cannot see it.

items.q: Which of these is a solid?
items.e: A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume.

items.q: Is flour a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Tiny solid grains pour, but each keeps its shape.

items.q: What is matter?
c: anything that has mass and takes up space
items.e: Air is matter too.

items.q: Is an ice cube a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: It has a definite shape and a definite volume.

items.q: Which state of matter has a fixed shape and a fixed volume?
items.e: Solids keep their shape.

items.q: Which of these is a solid?
items.e: A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume.

items.q: Is the bubbles in a fizzy drink a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: The bubbles are carbon dioxide gas.

items.q: Is water vapour a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Water vapour is a gas.

items.q: Is water a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Water is a liquid.

items.q: Which state of matter spreads out to fill any container?
items.e: Gas particles move freely.

items.q: Which property describes how easily a material bends without breaking?
items.e: Rubber is flexible.

items.q: What is it called when a gas turns into a liquid?
items.e: Water drops form on a cold glass.

items.q: Why is a stainless steel pot good for cooking?
c: It conducts heat well and does not melt on the stove.
items.e: Material choice depends on properties.

items.q: Is shampoo a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Shampoo is a liquid.

items.q: Which state of matter flows and takes the shape of its container?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: Is soya sauce a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: It has a definite volume but no definite shape.

items.q: Which state of matter takes the shape of its container but keeps its volume?
items.e: Liquids flow.

items.q: Is orange juice a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Orange juice is a liquid.

items.q: Is the gas in a balloon a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: It has no definite shape and no definite volume.

items.q: What happens to the particles in water when it boils?
c: They move faster and spread far apart.
items.e: Heating gives particles more energy.

items.q: What is it called when a liquid turns into a gas?
items.e: Puddles dry up by evaporation.

items.q: How are the particles arranged in a gas?
c: close together but able to slide past each other
far apart and moving quickly in all directions
packed closely in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
items.e: Everything is made of tiny particles.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: Smoke has mass and takes up space, so it is matter. Light, heat, sound and shadows are not matter.

items.q: Which of these is not matter?
items.e: A shadow has no mass and does not take up space, so it is not matter. Smoke is matter: it is made of particles.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: Milk has mass and takes up space, so it is matter. Light, heat, sound and shadows are not matter.

items.q: Which of these is not matter?
items.e: A rainbow has no mass and does not take up space, so it is not matter. Steam is matter: it is made of particles.

items.q: In which state are the particles far apart and moving quickly in all directions?
items.e: Everything is made of tiny particles.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: A cloud has mass and takes up space, so it is matter. Light, heat, sound and shadows are not matter.

items.q: Which of these is not matter?
items.e: A thought has no mass and does not take up space, so it is not matter. Oxygen gas is matter: it is made of particles.

items.q: Which of these is not matter?
items.e: Heat has no mass and does not take up space, so it is not matter. Dust is matter: it is made of particles.

items.q: Look at how close the particles are. Which state of matter is this?

items.q: What state of matter is a mystery material in, according to this model?
items.e: In a solid the particles are packed tightly in a pattern and only vibrate in place.

items.q: Which of these is not matter?

items.q: Ice cubes form in a freezer tray. Which change of state is this?
items.e: Is it getting hotter or colder? Which state does it start and end in?

items.q: Your breath makes tiny droplets on a cold window. Which change of state is this?

a gas changing into a liquid when it is cooled
a liquid changing into a gas when it is heated quickly

items.e: Is it getting hotter or colder? Which state does it start and end in?

items.e: Melting, freezing, evaporating (and boiling), condensing.

items.q: Which property can you measure with a balance?
items.e: A balance compares masses.

items.q: Wet washing dries on a line. Which change of state is this?
items.e: Is it getting hotter or colder? Which state does it start and end in?

items.q: Which object is an electrical insulator?
items.e: A plastic straw does not let electricity flow through it. All the other objects are metals, which are conductors.

items.q: Obinna shines a torch on a rock to see if it sparkles. Which property is he testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's reflectivity.

items.q: Which of these does not dissolve in water?
items.e: Cooking oil does not dissolve. You can still see it in the water, or it settles to the bottom or floats on top.

items.q: Hadiza puts a spoon in a circuit to see if the bulb lights. Which property is she testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's electrical conductivity.

items.q: Which object will a magnet pick up?
items.e: An iron key ring contains iron, so it is attracted to a magnet. Many metals, like aluminium, copper and gold, are not.

items.q: Which object will a magnet pick up?
items.e: An iron nail contains iron, so it is attracted to a magnet. Many metals, like aluminium, copper and gold, are not.

items.q: Which of these does not dissolve in water?
items.e: Chalk dust does not dissolve. You can still see it in the water, or it settles to the bottom.

items.q: A bulb is in a circuit with a gap. Which object placed across the gap will make the bulb light?
items.e: Metals conduct electricity. A wooden pencil is an insulator.

items.q: Which of these does not dissolve in water?
items.e: Small pebbles does not dissolve. You can still see it in the water, or it settles to the bottom.

items.q: Which of these dissolves in water?
items.e: Baking soda dissolves: it breaks into particles too small to see and spreads through the water.

items.q: Nkechi drops a stone into a graduated cylinder of water. Which property is she testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's volume.

items.q: Bisi puts a sample on a balance. Which property is she testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's mass.

items.q: Which object will a magnet pick up?
items.e: A steel paper clip contains iron, so it is attracted to a magnet. Many metals, like aluminium, copper and gold, are not.

items.q: A bulb is in a circuit with a gap. Which object placed across the gap will make the bulb light?
items.e: Metals conduct electricity. A rubber eraser is an insulator.

items.q: Which of these does not dissolve in water?
items.e: Cornstarch does not dissolve. You can still see it in the water, or it settles to the bottom.

items.q: Which metal object will not stick to a magnet?
items.e: A US penny is a metal, but it has no iron in it, so a magnet does not attract it. Iron and steel are attracted to magnets.

items.q: Abdullahi rubs a metal coin and watches it shine under a lamp. Which property is he testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's reflectivity.

items.q: Which object is an electrical insulator?
items.e: A glass marble does not let electricity flow through it. All the other objects are metals, which are conductors.

items.q: Dayo drops a sugar cube into warm tea and waits. Which property is he testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's solubility.

items.q: A bulb is in a circuit with a gap. Which object placed across the gap will make the bulb light?
items.e: Metals conduct electricity. A glass marble is an insulator.

items.q: A class leaves two dishes of salt water in the sun. One dish is covered with plastic wrap. After 3 days, which dish has dry salt crystals?
items.e: In the open dish the water vapour escapes into the air. Under the wrap the vapour is trapped and drips back down.

items.q: Which model shows what happens when salt dissolves in water?
c: Salt particles spread out between the water particles.
Salt particles turn into water particles.
items.e: The salt particles break apart and mix in among the water particles. Both kinds are still there.

items.q: How could you show that a gas has mass?
c: Weigh a flat football, pump it up, and weigh it again.
items.e: More air, more mass.

items.q: A jeweler wants to test if a gold ring is real without damaging it. Which test is best?
c: Check if it is attracted to a magnet (real gold is not).
items.e: Real gold is not magnetic. If a magnet pulls it, the ring has iron or steel in it.

items.q: Gbenga blows up two balloons the same size. He puts one in a warm room and one outside on a cold night. What happens to the outside balloon?
items.e: Cooling makes the air particles move more slowly and take up less space.

items.q: Segun says that when sugar dissolves, it is destroyed. Which evidence best shows he is wrong?
c: The mass of the water plus sugar stays the same before and after stirring.
items.e: If the sugar were destroyed, the mass would go down. It stays the same, so the sugar is still there as tiny particles.

items.q: A flat bike tyre has a mass of 452 g. After it is pumped full of air, its mass is 463 g. What is the mass of the air inside?
items.e: 463 − 452 = 11 g. The air added mass, so air is matter.

items.q: Why is toothpaste hard to classify?
c: It holds its shape a little but flows when squeezed, so it has properties of solids and liquids.
items.e: Some materials are tricky.

items.q: A flat beach ball has a mass of 594 g. After it is pumped full of air, its mass is 602 g. What is the mass of the air inside?
items.e: 602 − 594 = 8 g. The air added mass, so air is matter.

items.q: Tolu wants to find out which material is the best thermal insulator for a lunch box. What should she keep the same in her test?
c: only the colour of the boxes
the starting temperature and amount of the food, and the time
items.e: Only the material should change. Everything else must stay the same for a fair test.

items.q: A flat football ball has a mass of 408 g. After it is pumped full of air, its mass is 423 g. What is the mass of the air inside?
items.e: 423 − 408 = 15 g. The air added mass, so air is matter.

items.q: Victor tests whether salt dissolves faster in warm or cold water. Which plan is a fair test?
c: Use the same amount of salt and water in two cups, changing only the temperature.
Use more salt in the warm cup.
Use different cups and different amounts.
items.e: Change only one variable (temperature). Keep the salt, water and stirring the same.

items.q: A class weighs a sealed bag with ice, then weighs it again when the ice has melted. Why must the bag be sealed?
c: so no water can leak out or evaporate
items.e: If water escaped, the mass would go down and the test would be unfair.

items.q: Why does a smell spread across a room?
c: Smells are not made of particles.
Gas particles move and spread out in all directions.
items.e: Gas particles move freely.

items.q: A class wants to know which material makes the best wire for a circuit. Which property should they test?
items.e: A wire must carry electricity well, so test how well each material conducts.

items.q: Ruth puts a balloon on the neck of a bottle and moves the bottle from hot water into ice water. What happens to the balloon?
c: It shrinks, because the air particles slow down and move closer together.
items.e: Cooling slows the particles, so the air takes up less space and the balloon goes flat.

items.q: Nkechi's mystery liquid freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C. Which liquid is it most likely?
items.e: Pure water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C. The temperatures where a substance changes state help identify it.

items.q: A flat ball has a mass of 568 g. After it is pumped full of air, its mass is 575 g. What is the mass of the air inside?
items.e: 575 − 568 = 7 g. The air added mass, so air is matter.

items.q: How could you show that air takes up space?
c: Push an upside-down cup into water: the air stops the water filling it.
items.e: Gases take up space.
